d.title: Two attempts, and the second one had a sentence the first did not
d.caption: The judge's complaint — *“did not say where the money goes”* — became a lesson in the store, and the retry solved with **1 lesson** in its prompt and passed. **Nothing in the loop changed except the number of lessons available to it**, which is what makes the pattern cheap to try: no fine-tuning, no gradient, no new node — one `store.put` on the failure path and one read before solving.

state: '30 days, to the original payment method'

d.title: No weights change; the improvement is a sentence in the context
d.caption: That is the whole idea, and it is why the pattern is **cheap to try and hard to evaluate**. The lesson is text, written by the model, stored outside the run, prepended to the next attempt. **Nothing about the mechanism distinguishes a generalisable lesson from a wrong one, because both are sentences that get prepended** — and the store has no notion of which kind it is holding.

nodes.label: And hard to evaluate
nodes.sub: a wrong lesson is also a sentence

d.title: The payoff and the measurement problem are the same event
d.caption: A **different** question passed on the first attempt with the lesson in its prompt — which is transfer, and it is the point of the pattern. It is also where the evaluation gap is: **the judge confirmed the answer, not the lesson. Nothing in the loop checks that the lesson generalises**, so a lesson that happens to help on question two and misleads on question seven produces one visible success and one invisible failure.

nodes.label: So a misleading lesson is invisible

d.title: A conclusion from one example, phrased as a general rule
d.caption: 9.6 listed *remember wrong* as the worst memory failure — a mistaken fact persisting across every future conversation with nobody looking, because the system is doing exactly what it was told. **Reflexion hits it hardest, because the lesson was written by the model from a single failure: it is overfitted by construction**, and then applied to everything. Hence the three requirements — and **nothing else removes a bad lesson.**

nodes.label: Cap how many are injected
nodes.sub: or the prompt fills with them

nodes.label: An expiry or review path
nodes.sub: nothing else removes a bad one

d.title: The judge is the requirement, and self-judging is measurably unsafe here
d.caption: Without a reliable pass/fail signal there is nothing to reflect on — and 7.4 measured exactly where self-judging breaks: **a model scored a claim its own document contradicted at +5.293, strongly positive.** So **a self-judged reflexion loop can write lessons from failures it misdiagnosed, which is worse than not reflecting at all**, because the bad lesson then persists. Where it works: tests, schemas, status codes.

nodes.label: The signal is the difficulty
nodes.sub: no judge, nothing to reflect on

nodes.label: Which is where the benchmarks come from

d.title: One step per worker, and no history at all
d.caption: Each worker's input is a **single** `HumanMessage`. So the prompt does not grow with the task's length — against 11.3's ReAct, where every turn carries every previous thought and result. **And it cuts both ways: a worker cannot adapt, because it does the step it was given whether or not that step still makes sense after the previous one returned something unexpected.** The commitment that makes cost predictable is the commitment that makes it rigid.

d.title: The same trade, read from both ends
d.caption: **If the steps are knowable before starting, planning once is cheaper and more reliable. If the next step depends on what the last one returned, a plan is a guess that will be wrong** — which is 11.1's sequence-against-choice test applied one level up. Note the row that matters for budgeting: `1 + len(plan)` is a number you can put in a design document, and `2..N` is not.

d.title: Two replans, and a bug that only exists on this path
d.caption: A plan made before seeing any results will sometimes be wrong, so the replan path is what makes the pattern usable — **and it needs a budget, because a task the planner cannot solve replans forever, now with a planning call per iteration on top of the wasted worker calls.** The trap: **on replan `done` already holds the failed step's output, so the new plan's indices no longer line up with `len(done)`** and the executor picks the wrong step.

d.title: Predictable decomposition on one side, a short or dependent task on the other
d.caption: It wins where the task decomposes predictably — a report with known sections — where the **steps are independent so they can run in parallel** via 10.2's `Send`, and where **you want a plan a human can approve before execution** (9.8), which only a declared plan makes possible. It is wrong when the first step's result changes the second, when **planning two steps is a model call spent to avoid a model call**, and when every run replans anyway.

d.title: Three queries, and the machinery cost nothing on the first
d.caption: The good path is the one worth noticing: **0.443 graded good and went straight to generate, so the extra structure cost nothing on a query the baseline already handled.** The rewrite path is 7.2's measured case — **0.139 to 0.709**, with `bill-cancel-sub` replacing the order-cancellation document. And 7.2's caveat holds: that rewrite was written knowing the corpus, and a blind rewriter landed **0 of 5** attempts on one query.

steps.code: 'how long do you keep my information'

d.title: Three graders, and each inherits a limitation measured in module 7
d.caption: **The pattern cannot be better than its grader**, and every available grader carries a known flaw. The cross-encoder case is the sharpest: **using it as a grader would refuse precisely the queries dense retrieval handles correctly, so it would send working retrievals down the rewrite path** — two models failing on the same query class are not an ensemble (7.1).

items.label: A score threshold
items.desc: 7.1's AUC 0.943 — and the populations overlap, so it is a chosen trade rather than a classifier.

items.label: A cross-encoder
items.desc: Refuses the queries dense retrieval answers correctly (7.1) — a second opinion, not a better one.

items.label: An LLM grader
items.desc: 7.4 measured a model scoring a contradiction at +5.293 — relevance is not correctness.

d.title: Grade cheaply first, and spend a model call only on failure
d.caption: Worst case per query is retrieve, grade, rewrite, retrieve, grade, generate — **with an LLM grader that is three model calls before generation, on every query, including the ones 7.2 measured the baseline answering at MRR 0.964.** The gate is 7.2's conclusion expressed as a graph: **the free threshold first, escalating only when it says the retrieval was weak.** A loop that grades expensively on every query has spent its budget on the queries that did not need it.

d.title: Two questions, four answers
d.caption: The first question eliminates most systems: **if the model does not need to decide anything, it is a chain, and most RAG pipelines are here** (8.1). The second is 11.1's test — sequence or choice — and only the last branch produces an agent loop. Note what the tree does **not** have: a branch that arrives at ReAct because the task is important, or because an agent was asked for.

children.label: Can you plan it up front?

d.title: Three modifiers, each answering a different question from the tree
d.caption: **This is the part the decision table hides: reflection, reflexion and agentic RAG are not rungs on the ladder, they are modifiers you add to whichever rung you landed on.** A router can have agentic RAG behind one branch; a plan-and-execute worker can reflect on its output. So the tree picks the control structure, and these three answer a separate question about **which part is unreliable.**

d.title: Six guards, and five of them live in two places
d.caption: Read the right-hand column: **four of the six are the router's job, because the router is the only place that can make a decision rather than raise.** The give-up node is the exception and the one most often missing — **it is what turns “the agent failed” into a response you can show a user.** And `recursion_limit` is last on purpose: a backstop for what the other five did not anticipate.

d.title: Six patterns on one task, and the cheapest one got the answer
d.caption: **Call + tools got the answer in one call, because the tool output was the answer** — and every row below it spends more to arrive at the same place, with reflection at **6**. Two caveats keep this honest: the single call answered **from memory**, so it is ungrounded (5.7), and the router's answer depended on the category being right (11.2). The ordering is the argument of the whole module.

d.title: Twenty real examples usually resolve to a router
d.caption: Read the table **upward** rather than downward — start at the cheapest row and stop at the first one that works. And the practical corollary is a conversation rather than a technique: **when a stakeholder asks for an agent, ask for twenty real examples of what it must handle. Most of the time they resolve to a handful of intents with one operation each, which is a router — and saying so early is worth more than any individual pattern in this module.**

nodes.label: Saying so early is the value
